title: Customising with Sass
summary: Sass is a tool that makes CSS before the page is shown. It lets you choose some Bootstrap values before building its styles.
introduction: Sass is a tool that makes CSS before the page is shown. It lets you choose some Bootstrap values before building its styles. Think of picking colours before mixing the paint. Change one theme value first, then learn where the imports belong.
learningObjectives: Set up a Sass build that imports Bootstrap's source from node_modules
Override default variables before the import to change colours, fonts and spacing
Add a theme colour and enable optional features with the $enable-* flags
Import only the parts of Bootstrap a project uses

blocks.text: Bootstrap is written in SCSS, the Sass syntax that looks like CSS with extras, and the file you load from the CDN is the compiled result. To compile your own you need the source, which comes with the npm package, and a compiler: the `sass` package (Dart Sass). Both install in one command. Keep your own file outside `node_modules` so updates never overwrite it.

blocks.title: Terminal
blocks.code:
npm install bootstrap@5.3.3 sass
mkdir scss dist
npx sass --quiet-deps scss/custom.scss dist/custom.css

blocks.title: Result
blocks.content:
The compiler prints nothing on success
dist/custom.css and dist/custom.css.map are written; link dist/custom.css in your HTML instead of the CDN stylesheet

blocks.text: `--quiet-deps` hides deprecation warnings from inside `node_modules`. Bootstrap 5.3 is written with Sass's older `@import` rule, which recent Dart Sass versions flag as deprecated; the output is still correct, and the flag keeps the terminal readable. Add `--watch` to recompile on every save.
Option A: override, then import everything

Every Bootstrap variable is declared with the `!default` flag, which means "use this value unless one already exists". So any variable you set **before** importing Bootstrap becomes the value the whole framework compiles with. The simplest custom build is a few assignments followed by one import of the complete framework.

blocks.title: scss/custom.scss
What changes in dist/custom.css
blocks.content:
Every primary element is purple: .btn-primary, .bg-primary, .text-primary, links, focus rings and the --bs-primary variables
The body font stack starts with Inter
Buttons, cards, inputs and alerts have .75rem rounded corners
The spacing scale grows: mt-3 is now 1.25rem and mt-5 is 3.75rem, and container padding and gutters scale with it
.hero gets 3.75rem of vertical padding, 6.25rem from 992px

blocks.text: Changing `$primary` here recolours *everything* derived from it, including the `--bs-btn-*` variables that the previous lesson had to override one by one. That is the difference between Sass and CSS variables: Sass runs before the derivation, CSS variables after.

blocks.title: Common mistake: overriding after the import
blocks.text: Put `$primary: #6f42c1;` *below* the `@import` line and nothing changes. By then Bootstrap has already given `$primary` its default and compiled every rule that uses it; your assignment only affects your own code further down. The order is always: your variables, then Bootstrap, then your rules. If you need Bootstrap's functions (such as `tint-color()`) inside an override, use the ordered import in the next section, because in Option A the functions do not exist yet when your overrides run.
Option B: ordered imports and a new theme colour

Adding a colour to the theme means changing a **map**, and maps can only be modified after Bootstrap's variables are defined but before the maps are turned into CSS. The documented order is: functions, your variable overrides, `variables` and `variables-dark`, your map overrides, then `maps`, `mixins`, `root` and the parts you want. Since 5.3 a theme colour also needs entries in the text-emphasis, subtle-background and subtle-border maps for both colour modes, because alerts and list groups read those variants.

blocks.title: scss/custom.scss with a tertiary colour
What dist/custom.css now contains
blocks.content:
New classes: .btn-tertiary, .btn-outline-tertiary, .bg-tertiary, .text-tertiary, .border-tertiary, .alert-tertiary, .bg-tertiary-subtle, .text-tertiary-emphasis and .border-tertiary-subtle, each with light and dark values
New variables: --bs-tertiary, --bs-tertiary-rgb, --bs-tertiary-text-emphasis, --bs-tertiary-bg-subtle, --bs-tertiary-border-subtle
No card, navbar, modal or form styles: those files were not imported, and the file is much smaller than the CDN build

blocks.text: Feature flags, breakpoints and the utility API

A set of `$enable-*` booleans switches whole features on or off at compile time: `$enable-shadows` adds subtle shadows to components, `$enable-gradients` adds gradient backgrounds, `$enable-negative-margins` generates the `m*-n*` classes, `$enable-rounded: false` removes every border radius, and `$enable-dark-mode: false` drops the dark colour mode entirely for a smaller file. Breakpoints and container widths are maps too (`$grid-breakpoints`, `$container-max-widths`) and can be edited the same way as the theme colours. New utilities come from the **utility API**: add an entry to the `$utilities` map between the `utilities` import and `utilities/api`.

blocks.title: Place flags with overrides; add the utility before utilities/api
What dist/custom.css now contains
blocks.content:
Buttons, cards and form controls carry box shadows
Negative margin classes such as .mt-n3 and .ms-n2 exist
Three new utilities: .cursor-auto, .cursor-pointer and .cursor-grab, each declared with !important like every other utility

blocks.text: Option B's step 6 is also a size optimisation: a landing page that uses the grid, type, buttons and utilities does not need the 20-odd component files. The required core is `functions`, `variables`, `variables-dark`, `maps`, `mixins` and `root`; everything else is optional, and `utilities/api` must stay last. The JavaScript can be trimmed the same way in a bundler by importing individual plugins, for example `import Modal from 'bootstrap/js/dist/modal'`, instead of the whole bundle.

rows: Nudge a few colours on a finished site
In the browser, after Bootstrap's CSS
Change the palette, fonts, radius or spacing scale everywhere
At build time, before Bootstrap compiles
Add a theme colour with all its classes

blocks.title: Keep the defaults file open
blocks.text: `node_modules/bootstrap/scss/_variables.scss` lists every variable with its default and the `!default` flag. Searching it is the fastest way to find the name of whatever you want to change, and reading how `$primary` feeds `$theme-colors` shows why map overrides must wait until after the variables are imported.

questions.question: Where must `$primary: #6f42c1;` appear in custom.scss to recolour the framework?
questions.explanation: Bootstrap declares its variables with !default, so a value defined earlier is kept. An override placed after the import is too late.

questions.question: Adding `"tertiary"` to the `$theme-colors` map generates classes such as `.btn-tertiary` and `.bg-tertiary` in the compiled CSS.
questions.explanation: Buttons, backgrounds, text and border utilities loop over $theme-colors. The 5.3 subtle and emphasis variants additionally need entries in the text, bg-subtle and border-subtle maps for both colour modes.

seo.title: Customising Bootstrap with Sass – Variables and Colours
seo.description: Customise Bootstrap 5.3 with Sass: override $primary, $spacer and fonts before the import, add a theme colour, set feature flags and import only what you need.
